concepts.label: Geography
concepts.learning_takeaway: Connect social and environmental processes through place.
concepts.card: Geography studies places through the connections between people and environments. Human geography examines societies and economies; physical geography examines landscapes and environmental processes. Bringing them together helps explain why places differ and how human actions contribute to local and global change.

concepts.card: A sestina reuses six end-words in a prescribed order across six six-line stanzas, then gathers them in a three-line envoi. Its organizing device is recurrence rather than ordinary rhyme. Changing contexts can give the same repeated word a different meaning each time.

concepts.card: Proportionality is a legal test relating a restriction to its justification. Under European Convention Article 8 review, officials must show a pressing social need and measures proportionate to a legitimate aim. Calling an interference useful does not by itself establish necessity.

concepts.label: Gamelan
concepts.learning_takeaway: Compare repertoire and performance setting within gamelan.
concepts.card: Gamelan encompasses ensemble music traditions with differing repertoires and settings. In Bali, gong kebyar uses rapidly changing tempi and interlocking parts; older ceremonial styles documented among Balinese communities in Lombok sound comparatively static. Comparing these settings reveals variation within the same musical tradition.
concepts.original_description: Exploring Indonesian ensemble traditions centered on tuned percussion.

evidence.note: Balinese ensemble and layered melodic context inspected.

relations.note: The article examines contrasting gamelan musical repertoires.

imported_records.description: Exploring Indonesian ensemble traditions centered on tuned percussion.

concepts.label: Acrostic
concepts.learning_takeaway: Read a vertical message inside the poem’s ordinary lines.
concepts.card: An acrostic hides a word or name in the initial letters of successive poetic lines. Reading down those letters reveals an additional message within the poem. In Blake’s “London,” the third stanza’s initials spell HEAR, reinforcing its attention to troubling sounds.

relations.note: The Academy explicitly identifies acrostic as a poetic form.

concepts.label: Adams square II projection
concepts.learning_takeaway: Compare square outlines with local conformality and area distortion.
concepts.card: Adams square II maps the world into a square, with the equator and central meridian forming diagonals in its original design. Local angles are preserved except at the corners. Strong area exaggeration near the poles and antimeridian limits what its neat outline conveys.

relations.note: Esri identifies Adams square II as a map projection.

concepts.label: Cento
concepts.learning_takeaway: Explore how juxtaposition transforms borrowed poetic lines.
concepts.card: A cento is a poem assembled entirely from lines by other poets. Its composition depends on selection and juxtaposition: familiar voices meet in unfamiliar combinations, creating irony or humor. The borrowed lines remain recognizable ingredients while their new arrangement creates another poem.

relations.note: The Academy explicitly identifies cento as a poetic form.

concepts.label: Chaski (Inca messenger)
concepts.learning_takeaway: Connect portable records with an imperial messenger network.
concepts.card: Chaskis were official messengers in the Inca Empire. Khipus could be wrapped into portable bundles for them to carry across its territory. The example shows how a system of recorded information depended on transport as well as the cords used to encode it.

relations.note: Editorial imperial-administration placement; NIST identifies official Inca messengers.

concepts.label: Chine collé
concepts.learning_takeaway: See paper tone as part of the printed image.
concepts.card: Chine collé prints an image on thin paper adhered to a thicker backing during printing. Starch adhesive and pressure join the sheets, while the thin paper’s tone and surface affect the image. Redon’s gray paper supplies a background hue in The Buddha.

relations.note: Chine collé is explicitly defined as a printing process.

concepts.label: Chöd
concepts.learning_takeaway: Connect offering practice with investigation of self clinging.
concepts.card: Chöd is a Buddhist offering practice directed at cutting self clinging. In Lama Zopa’s teaching, ritual offerings of the body to spirits are connected with examining the apparently inherent self. Fear becomes an occasion to investigate that self’s supposed independent existence.

relations.note: The teaching situates chöd within Buddhist charity and wisdom.

concepts.label: Civilian Public Service (US, World War II)
concepts.learning_takeaway: Examine unpaid civilian work as a historical pacifist alternative.
concepts.card: During World War II, US Civilian Public Service offered conscientious objectors work outside military command. Government authorization combined with funding and administration by peace churches. At Patapsco, participants maintained parks and fought fires without wages, showing the practical costs of this route for pacifists.

evidence.locator: Civilian Public Service; In Camp; Challenges, lines 44–59

relations.note: Editorial application of pacifism based on documented conscientious-objector service.

concepts.label: Clerihew
concepts.learning_takeaway: Use irregular rhythm to make a comic miniature biography.
concepts.card: A clerihew makes a comic miniature biography from four uneven lines rhyming aabb. The subject’s name appears among the first couplet’s rhyming words. Its deliberately awkward rhythm helps turn a famous person’s life into a playful, deadpan portrait.

evidence.locator: Definition and From A Poet’s Glossary, lines 28–33

relations.note: The Academy describes clerihew as a comic poetic form.

concepts.label: Contributory injustice
concepts.learning_takeaway: Distinguish refused knowledge from an undeveloped shared concept.
concepts.card: Contributory injustice, in Dotson’s account, occurs when a dominant group refuses interpretive resources that marginalized communities have already developed. The issue is not simply a missing concept. Knowledge can be available within a community yet excluded from the understanding accepted by others.

evidence.locator: §4.1 Epistemic Injustice, Dotson and Pohlhaus paragraphs, lines 225–228

relations.note: The entry explicitly classifies contributory injustice as epistemic injustice.

concepts.label: Dhikr
concepts.learning_takeaway: Recognize repeated remembrance across varied devotional forms.
concepts.card: Dhikr is devotional remembrance in Sufism, often performed through rhythmic recitation of God’s names or litanies. Some forms include poetry, dance or instruments. The repeated vocal pattern organizes worship, while the varying accompaniments show that remembrance has several forms of expression.

relations.note: The definition explicitly identifies dhikr as Sufi devotion.

concepts.label: Double dactyl
concepts.learning_takeaway: Fit comic content to rhythm and a single long word.
concepts.card: A double dactyl is light verse in two four-line stanzas. Most lines contain two feet, each with a stressed syllable followed by two unstressed ones. Nonsense, a person’s name, one six-syllable word and shorter rhyming endings create a compact compositional puzzle.

relations.note: The university instructional page identifies this as a verse form.

concepts.label: Margin of appreciation (European human-rights law)
concepts.learning_takeaway: Connect national discretion with continuing judicial review.
concepts.card: The margin of appreciation is discretion allowed to national authorities in European human rights review. They initially assess a restriction’s necessity, but the Court can review their decision. Its breadth varies with the issues and interests involved, so discretion does not settle legality.

evidence.locator: Is the interference necessary in a democratic society?, paragraphs 34–36, printed pages 15–16

relations.note: Article 8 review permits qualified national discretion.

concepts.label: Pilot judgment procedure (European Court of Human Rights)
concepts.learning_takeaway: Link individual cases with remedies for a systemic problem.
concepts.card: The pilot judgment procedure lets the European Court of Human Rights address structural problems behind repetitive applications. It selects representative cases and indicates remedial measures to governments. Related cases may be paused while national action proceeds, with examination resumable when justice requires.

evidence.locator: What is the pilot judgment procedure?, printed page 1, lines 4–18

relations.note: Pilot judgments address systemic violations of Convention rights.

concepts.label: Equal Earth projection
concepts.learning_takeaway: Compare areas without mistaking preserved size for preserved shape.
concepts.card: Equal Earth is a world-map projection that preserves relative areas while distorting shapes, angles, and distances. This makes it useful for thematic maps comparing area characteristics: a region’s mapped size remains meaningful even when its outline changes.

relations.note: Esri explicitly identifies Equal Earth as a map projection.

concepts.label: Euclidean buffering
concepts.learning_takeaway: Identify when flat-map distance zones inherit projection distortion.
concepts.card: Euclidean buffering draws a distance zone using straight-line measurements on a flat coordinate plane. It works best around features concentrated within a suitably projected small region. Where the projection distorts distance substantially, equal map offsets no longer represent equal distances on Earth.

evidence.locator: “Euclidean and geodesic buffering”, method bullets and shape-preserving Geodesic option

relations.note: Esri names Euclidean buffering as a geographic buffer construction method.

concepts.label: Fitting-attitude theories of value
concepts.learning_takeaway: Distinguish a deserved response from an actual feeling.
concepts.card: Fitting-attitude theories explain value through responses that an object merits. Being admirable, for example, is explained through the fittingness of admiration. The claim concerns appropriate responses, not whatever people happen to feel, so actual affection or dislike alone does not settle an object’s value.

relations.note: The entry explicitly presents these as theories explaining value.

concepts.label: Gamelan gong kebyar
concepts.learning_takeaway: Hear musical dynamics while checking performance context.
concepts.card: Gamelan gong kebyar is a Balinese ensemble style that emerged in northern Bali around 1915. Rapid tempo changes and dynamic interlocking parts distinguish its repertoire. An album labeled court music illustrates a contextual trap: most documented performances belonged to other settings.

relations.note: Gong kebyar is identified as a gamelan style.

concepts.label: Geodesic buffering
concepts.learning_takeaway: Separate curved-surface distance from flat-map appearance.
concepts.card: Geodesic buffering builds distance zones while accounting for Earth’s curved spheroidal surface. It is useful over large extents and near poles or the date line. A zone may look distorted on a flat map while showing the intended distance correctly on a globe.

evidence.locator: “Euclidean and geodesic buffering”, method bullets and shape-preserving Geodesic option

relations.note: Esri names geodesic buffering as a geographic buffer construction method.

concepts.label: Goode homolosine projection
concepts.learning_takeaway: Understand how interruptions trade continuity for reduced shape distortion.
concepts.card: For a spherical Earth, Goode homolosine combines sinusoidal and Mollweide projections to preserve areas. Its familiar interrupted versions split the map into lobes emphasizing land or oceans. These cuts reduce the shape distortion found near the edges of its uninterrupted form.

relations.note: Esri identifies Goode homolosine as a map projection.

concepts.label: Gyotaku
concepts.learning_takeaway: Connect transferred detail with paint quantity and surface contact.
concepts.card: Gyotaku transfers a fish’s surface to paper by rubbing it over an inked specimen. The print records details of shape and texture. In a Smithsonian educational version, rubber replicas replace real fish; excessive paint blurs the transfer, making material quantity part of the result.

relations.note: Documented ink and paper transfer supports this printmaking placement.

concepts.label: Haibun
concepts.learning_takeaway: Read prose and haiku through their implicit connection.
concepts.card: Haibun combines prose and haiku, a literary form originating in Japan. The prose often describes an environment and precedes a poem whose connection remains implicit. In Bashō’s travel writing, the surrounding narrative and individual haiku create meaning together without spelling out every link.

evidence.locator: Definition; “From A Poet’s Glossary”, prose–haiku relationship

relations.note: The Academy identifies haibun as a literary poetic form.

concepts.label: Hermeneutical injustice
concepts.learning_takeaway: Locate an interpretive obstacle within unequal shared resources.
concepts.card: In Fricker’s account, hermeneutical injustice arises when unequal shared interpretive resources leave someone unfairly unable to understand a social experience. Sexual harassment before that concept gained recognition illustrates the problem: the obstacle lies partly in collective understanding, rather than only one listener’s disbelief.

evidence.locator: Printed page 1, hermeneutical-injustice definition and harassment example

relations.note: Fricker explicitly identifies this form of epistemic injustice.

concepts.label: Hotine oblique Mercator projection
concepts.learning_takeaway: Match a conformal projection to an oblique region.
concepts.card: Hotine oblique Mercator aligns a conformal map with a region extending diagonally rather than north–south or east–west. It preserves angles and shapes locally, but area and distance distortion increase away from the central region. Orientation therefore matters when choosing a regional projection.

relations.note: Esri identifies Hotine oblique Mercator as a map projection.

concepts.label: Complementarity (International Criminal Court)
concepts.learning_takeaway: Evaluate genuine domestic proceedings before ICC admissibility.
concepts.card: Complementarity gives the International Criminal Court a role alongside national criminal justice. Under the inspected Rome Statute, genuine domestic investigation or prosecution can make a case inadmissible. Proceedings that shield a suspect illustrate unwillingness; other jurisdiction and admissibility conditions also apply.

relations.note: Articles 1 and 17 establish the ICC’s complementary role.

concepts.label: Ignatian Examen
concepts.learning_takeaway: Use daily events as material for reflective prayer.
concepts.card: The Ignatian Examen is Christian prayer through reflection on daily experience. One adapted sequence begins with awareness of God, reviews gratitude and emotions, then prays over one feature of the day and looks toward tomorrow. Ordinary events become material for discernment.

evidence.locator: Main explanation and five-step method, lines 85–98

relations.note: The source describes an adapted Christian prayer method.

concepts.label: Tokuseu Hitome Sohshibori Hon Furisode (Met 1997.228)
concepts.learning_takeaway: Trace a planned dye pattern across garment seams.
concepts.card: Takuo Itoh’s 1995 furisode kimono demonstrates shibori at the scale of an entire garment. A continuous dyed pattern crosses the back seam and extends from body to sleeves. Planning on fabric of fixed width aligns areas that garment construction later joins.

relations.note: The museum explicitly identifies this garment’s shibori technique.

concepts.label: Jus cogens
aliases: Peremptory norms of general international law
concepts.learning_takeaway: Recognize limits on treaty agreement.
concepts.card: Jus cogens denotes peremptory norms accepted by the international community of states as a whole, permitting no derogation. Under Vienna Convention Article 53, a treaty conflicting with such a norm when concluded is void; ordinary agreement cannot override it.

relations.note: Peremptory norms constrain international law.

concepts.label: Kanoko shibori
concepts.learning_takeaway: Connect individual bindings with a repeated dot pattern.
concepts.card: Kanoko shibori is a resist dyeing method that binds small pinches of cloth before dyeing. Releasing the ties produces tiny undyed details, often squares with central dots. A Met robe illustrates how many individually tied units create an extensive patterned surface.

relations.note: The Met describes kanoko as a shibori variant.

concepts.label: Khipu
concepts.learning_takeaway: Read decimal organization in knots while retaining interpretive uncertainty.
concepts.card: Khipus recorded information in the Inca Empire through cords and knots. Knot positions can represent decimal places, while twists, attachments, and colors provide further distinctions whose meanings scholars investigate. Numerical organization therefore depends on a cord’s structure, rather than an alphabetic sequence of written words.

evidence.locator: What is a khipu?; Encoding the Khipu; Khipu Uses, lines 132–157 and 195

relations.note: NIST documents khipu use throughout the Inca Empire.

concepts.label: Kintsugi
concepts.learning_takeaway: Understand visible repair as an artistic treatment of damage.
concepts.card: Kintsugi is the Japanese art of repairing broken ceramics with gold lacquer. The repair restores function while giving damage a visible artistic role. The Met interprets this treatment as enhancing a prized object’s value, a curatorial judgment rather than a universal price rule.

relations.note: The exhibition identifies kintsugi within Japanese ceramic art.

concepts.label: Koan
concepts.learning_takeaway: Distinguish a contemplative question from an explanatory answer.
concepts.card: A koan is a paradoxical question that a Zen teacher gives a student for meditation. Its purpose is to interrupt habitual analytical thinking rather than supply an ordinary explanatory answer. The tradition treats this encounter as a possible route toward realization.

relations.note: Zen meditation context motivates this Buddhist practice placement.

concepts.label: Kotekan
concepts.learning_takeaway: Hear the composite melody across paired parts.
concepts.card: Kotekan is an interlocking technique in Balinese gamelan. Two musicians divide rapid melodic figures into separate parts whose combination maintains rhythmic continuity. The result belongs to the composition’s melody: listening to either player alone misses the continuous composite line.

relations.note: Tenzer identifies kotekan within Balinese gamelan texture.

concepts.label: Kulintang Kultura: Danongan Kalanduyan and Gong Music of the Philippine Diaspora
concepts.learning_takeaway: Compare inheritance and transformation across the album’s discs.
concepts.card: Kulintang Kultura honors musician and teacher Danongan Kalanduyan through two contrasting discs. His ensemble performs traditional Philippine gong music on the first; diaspora artists combine kulintang with contemporary genres on the second. Their juxtaposition makes musical inheritance and transformation audible within one collection.

relations.note: The album documents traditional and diaspora kulintang music.

concepts.label: Kulintang music
concepts.learning_takeaway: Compare traditional repertoire with diaspora adaptations.
concepts.card: Kulintang is a gong chime music tradition of the Philippines. The Kulintang Kultura album contrasts traditional ensemble repertoire with diaspora musicians’ combinations of kulintang and electronic, hip hop, rock and jazz styles. Hearing both reveals preservation through changing musical arrangements.

evidence.locator: Lesson introduction and learning objectives, lines 440–455

evidence.note: Traditional and contemporary repertoire comparison inspected.

relations.note: The lesson identifies kulintang as Philippine gong chime music.

concepts.label: Kundiman
concepts.learning_takeaway: Connect triple meter and melodic flow with devotion.
concepts.card: Kundiman is a Filipino song form in triple meter. In Felipe De Leon’s account, flowing melodies and subtle second beat syncopation loosen the beat’s pull. Devotion can address a partner, family, spiritual figure or motherland, extending the form beyond romantic love.

relations.note: The essay identifies kundiman as a musical form.

concepts.label: L’Estampe Originale
concepts.learning_takeaway: Connect artistic experimentation with professional printers’ expertise.
concepts.card: L’Estampe Originale was a print portfolio issued in nine installments from 1893 to 1895. Its range of media depended on collaboration between artists and professional printers. These partnerships enabled technical experiments, making the printer’s expertise part of artistic production.

relations.note: The portfolio collected collaborative experimental printmaking.

concepts.label: Lukasa memory board (Met 1977.467.3)
concepts.learning_takeaway: Examine how this carved board supports trained historical interpretation.
concepts.card: This Luba memory board communicates through incised designs and relief carving, whereas many other lukasa use attached beads and shells. The Met’s interpretation connects its motifs with political history and territory. Senior Mbudye members learned to decipher the board within a specialized knowledge tradition.

evidence.locator: Curatorial description, lines 10–16; Artwork Details, object number 1977.467.3

concepts.label: Mbudye association
concepts.learning_takeaway: Connect specialized historical knowledge with checks on chiefly power.
concepts.card: Mbudye is a Luba association charged with preserving and interpreting political and historical principles. Its councils could check or reinforce chiefly power. Members progressed through levels of knowledge, with those at the highest level authorized to interpret the intricate designs of lukasa memory boards.

relations.note: Editorial placement based on the association’s documented Luba state role.

concepts.label: Metaphysical grounding
concepts.learning_takeaway: Separate constitutive dependence from causal history.
concepts.card: Metaphysical grounding asks what makes a fact hold in virtue of another, rather than what caused it earlier. Philosophers use picketing as constituting a strike to illustrate the distinction. The disputed notion concerns constitutive explanation or determination, not just a necessary connection.

relations.note: The entry explicitly locates grounding questions within metaphysics.

concepts.label: Natural Earth projection
concepts.learning_takeaway: Recognize distortion within a rounded world-map compromise.
concepts.card: Natural Earth is a compromise world-map projection with rounded corners. It preserves neither areas nor angles exactly. High-latitude regions appear enlarged, while angular distortion increases toward the edges, showing why an attractive general-purpose map still requires care when comparing regions.

relations.note: Esri identifies Natural Earth as a world-map projection.

concepts.label: The Negro Motorist Green Book
concepts.learning_takeaway: Trace how shared information supported travel under segregation.
concepts.card: Published between 1936 and 1966, with a wartime interruption, the Green Book listed businesses welcoming African American travelers. Reports from readers and postal-worker contacts helped build its directory. Hotels, restaurants, and service stations turned shared local knowledge into a practical response to segregation.

relations.note: Editorial historical placement based on the documented segregation context.

concepts.label: Nembutsu
concepts.learning_takeaway: Recognize gratitude as the chant’s described devotional function.
concepts.card: Nembutsu is a Buddhist chanting practice. At the Buddhist Temple of Marin, a Jodo Shinshu community, chanting Namo Amida Butsu expresses gratitude. The temple places this chant alongside listening and compassionate living, illustrating a devotional function within one specific Buddhist tradition.

relations.note: The temple identifies Nembutsu within its Buddhist practices.

concepts.label: Non-refoulement
concepts.learning_takeaway: Connect protection before recognition with instrument-specific rules.
concepts.card: Non-refoulement protects people against return to prohibited danger. UNHCR’s account explains that refugee protection can apply before formal status recognition: returning an applicant prematurely could defeat it. Applicable dangers and exceptions depend on the governing refugee or human rights instrument.

evidence.locator: Legal basis, Beneficiaries and Exceptions, lines 44–79, 107–120

relations.note: The note locates non-refoulement in international refugee law.

concepts.label: Ottava rima
concepts.learning_takeaway: Follow alternating rhymes into a closing couplet.
concepts.card: Ottava rima organizes a stanza into eight lines rhyming abababcc, usually in iambic pentameter. After six lines alternate two rhymes, the closing couplet introduces a paired ending. The form can carry longer poems, including Byron’s Don Juan.

evidence.locator: “About Form”; CLERIHEW; DOUBLE-DACTYL; OTTAVA RIMA; SPENSERIAN STANZA

relations.note: The Poetry Archive explicitly identifies ottava rima as a stanza form.

concepts.label: Pacta sunt servanda
concepts.learning_takeaway: Connect binding force with performance.
concepts.card: Pacta sunt servanda requires parties to perform treaties in force in good faith. Article 26 of the Vienna Convention joins two obligations: a treaty binds its parties, and those parties must carry it out.

relations.note: The rule governs treaty performance.

concepts.label: Safe Conduct Pass in Phakpa script (Met 1993.256)
concepts.learning_takeaway: Read imperial authority through an inscription’s material construction.
concepts.card: This late-thirteenth-century Yuan safe-conduct pass carries an imperial inscription in Phakpa script. Silver fills an openwork design so its characters project on both sides, reversed on the back. The artifact connects official authority with the material construction and visibility of its written command.

evidence.locator: Curatorial description, lines 7–11; Artwork Details, object 1993.256

relations.note: Editorial Yuan-dynasty placement based on the museum’s object attribution.

concepts.label: Pansori
concepts.learning_takeaway: Trace narrative performance through singer and drummer.
concepts.card: Pansori is a Korean narrative vocal genre performed by one singer and one drummer. The singer develops an epic story through poetic, dramatic and musical expression. Sugungga illustrates how this small performing partnership can carry an extended tale with multiple characters.

relations.note: The program identifies pansori as a Korean vocal genre.

concepts.label: Peirce quincuncial projection
concepts.learning_takeaway: Distinguish map tiling from uniform distortion control.
concepts.card: Peirce quincuncial places the world inside a square that can tile a larger surface. It preserves local angles except at the middle of each edge, where areas become strongly exaggerated. A seamless-looking mosaic therefore does not imply uniformly low distortion.

relations.note: Esri identifies Peirce quincuncial as a map projection.

concepts.label: Pinpeat
concepts.learning_takeaway: Compare preservation and adaptation across community settings.
concepts.card: Pinpeat is Cambodia’s court music tradition. Smithsonian’s diaspora lesson asks how Cambodian American artists sustain and transform it in the United States. Studying both settings shows how cultural preservation can include adaptation as musicians encounter new social contexts.

evidence.locator: Lesson introduction and learning objectives, lines 440–455

relations.note: The lesson identifies pinpeat as Cambodian court music.

concepts.label: Port Chicago mutiny trial
concepts.learning_takeaway: Compare an unjust wartime conviction with later exoneration.
concepts.card: After the 1944 Port Chicago explosion, 258 Black sailors refused renewed ammunition-loading work; fifty were convicted of mutiny. Their case exposed the intersection of dangerous work and racial discrimination in the Navy. The Secretary of the Navy exonerated the sailors on July 17, 2024.

evidence.locator: The Aftermath and Mutiny; Trial Proceedings; Exoneration, lines 39–47 and 55

relations.note: Editorial placement based on documented segregation in the US Navy.

concepts.label: The Buddha (Odilon Redon lithograph, 1895)
concepts.learning_takeaway: Identify paper color’s contribution to this lithograph.
concepts.card: Odilon Redon’s 1895 lithograph The Buddha appeared in the ninth L’Estampe Originale album. Printed using chine collé, it combines black ink with light gray paper. The Met’s account shows how the paper itself contributes the image’s cool background tone.

evidence.locator: Print identification and curatorial explanation, lines 42–45

relations.note: The Buddha is identified in the portfolio’s ninth album.

concepts.label: Sanké Môn
concepts.learning_takeaway: Connect a collective ritual with its environmental setting.
concepts.card: Sanké Môn is an annual collective fishing ritual in San, Mali, commemorating the town’s foundation. Songs, dances, and other practices connect the gathering with local memory and belief. Protecting the Sanké pond preserves both an ecological resource and the setting that sustains the ritual.

relations.note: UNESCO explicitly identifies Sanké Môn as a collective ritual.

concepts.label: Shibori
concepts.learning_takeaway: Relate three dimensional shaping to the resulting dye pattern.
concepts.card: Shibori is shaped resist dyeing: fabric is folded, gathered, bound or clamped into three dimensional forms before coloring. When the cloth is flattened, its pattern records both the shape and the pressure that restricted dye access. Structure becomes visible as surface design.

relations.note: The practitioner network defines shibori as shaped resist dyeing.

concepts.label: Shikantaza
concepts.learning_takeaway: Understand sitting as realization within Soto practice.
concepts.card: Shikantaza is the just sitting approach associated with Japanese Soto Zen. In this account, sitting properly in zazen is itself the right state of mind, rather than merely preparation for later enlightenment. The posture expresses realization within the tradition’s understanding.

relations.note: The definition presents shikantaza as an approach within zazen.

concepts.label: Subsequent practice in treaty interpretation
concepts.learning_takeaway: Identify agreement through later application.
concepts.card: Subsequent practice can inform treaty interpretation when later application establishes the parties’ agreement about meaning. Article 31 of the Vienna Convention requires that agreement, so an isolated later act cannot automatically settle a disputed interpretation.

relations.note: Treaty practice informs interpretation.

concepts.label: Sugungga
concepts.learning_takeaway: Follow the hare’s verbal reversal of royal power.
concepts.card: Sugungga, the Tale of the Hare, is a surviving pansori story. A tortoise lures a hare to a sick Dragon King who wants its liver. The hare escapes by claiming the organ remains in the forest, turning verbal ingenuity against royal power.

relations.note: Sugungga is explicitly listed among surviving pansori stories.

concepts.label: Taizé meditative singing
concepts.learning_takeaway: Connect repetition and preparation with shared prayer.
concepts.card: Taizé meditative singing uses short songs whose few words express faith. Repetition supports shared Christian prayer without requiring a precisely fixed duration. The community recommends learning songs beforehand so attention during prayer can rest on listening and contemplation rather than instruction.

relations.note: Christian worship context motivates this prayer practice placement.

concepts.label: Tashlich
concepts.learning_takeaway: Distinguish ritual symbolism from feeding fish.
concepts.card: Tashlich is a Rosh Hashanah custom of prayer beside water and symbolic casting away of sins. Chabad’s account describes shaking garment corners as part of that symbolism. It distinguishes this ritual action from feeding fish, which is not the custom’s essential act.

relations.note: The article identifies Tashlich as a Rosh Hashanah custom.

concepts.label: Testimonial injustice
concepts.learning_takeaway: Identify prejudice within judgments of a speaker’s credibility.
concepts.card: In Fricker’s account, testimonial injustice occurs when prejudice makes a listener give someone’s words less credibility than they deserve. Her example is police disbelieving a Black speaker because of race. The wrong concerns recognition as a knower, not merely disagreement about a claim.

evidence.locator: Printed page 1, testimonial-injustice definition and police example

relations.note: Fricker explicitly identifies this form of epistemic injustice.

concepts.label: Treaty reservations
concepts.learning_takeaway: Recognize reservations and limits.
concepts.card: A treaty reservation is a state’s unilateral statement seeking to exclude or change provisions’ legal effect for itself. The Vienna Convention limits reservations, including those incompatible with a treaty’s object and purpose.

relations.note: Reservations qualify treaty provisions.

concepts.label: Triolet
concepts.learning_takeaway: Notice how a repeated line changes emotional force.
concepts.card: A triolet compresses a poem into eight lines and two rhymes. The opening line returns in lines four and seven; the second returns at the end. In Hardy’s “How Great My Grief,” repetition gains emotional weight as the surrounding questions change its force.

relations.note: The Academy explicitly identifies triolet as a fixed poetic form.

concepts.label: Tritina
concepts.learning_takeaway: Compare a compressed form with its sestina model.
concepts.card: A tritina contracts the sestina’s pattern of recurring end-words. Three end-words return across three three-line stanzas and meet in a final one-line envoi. Invented by Marie Ponsot, it concentrates formal repetition into a smaller space without abandoning the end-word constraint.

evidence.locator: “Rules of the Sestina Form”; final history paragraphs describing double sestina and tritina

relations.note: The Academy explicitly calls tritina a contraction of sestina.

concepts.label: Truthmaker maximalism
concepts.learning_takeaway: Test a universal truthmaker requirement against negative truths.
concepts.card: Truthmaker maximalism claims that every truth requires something in the world to make it true. The strain appears with negative truths: if absolutely nothing existed, what could make that true? This challenges the doctrine unless one rejects the possibility of an empty world.

relations.note: The entry identifies maximalism as a position within truthmaker theory.

concepts.label: Truthmaker theory
concepts.learning_takeaway: Connect truth to relevant reality rather than mere entailment.
concepts.card: Truthmaker theory asks how true representations depend on reality. A truthmaker must be relevant to what a claim is about, rather than merely entail it. What sits behind a refrigerator, for example, cannot explain why a truth of arithmetic holds.

evidence.locator: §1.1 Truthmaking as Entailment, relevance discussion; §1.2, lines 66–85

relations.note: The entry explicitly treats truthmaking as a metaphysical project.

concepts.label: Wrong kind of reason problem
concepts.learning_takeaway: Separate reasons to adopt an attitude from an object’s value.
concepts.card: The wrong kind of reason problem challenges certain fitting-attitude theories of value. A demon’s threat might give someone reason to value a worthless cup of mud. The incentive concerns having the attitude, while leaving the object’s value unexplained; theories must distinguish these reasons.

evidence.locator: §3.1 The Wrong Kind of Reason Problem, lines 167–175

relations.note: The entry explicitly identifies this challenge to fitting-attitude theories.
